parts.title: Compartments of the testes
paragraphs: The testes perform two linked jobs: they support sperm development and release hormones. Most sperm development occurs inside seminiferous tubules, the tightly coiled tubes within each testis. Developing germ cells lie among Sertoli cells in the tubule wall. Sertoli cells provide nutrients, organize the local environment and help regulate development. Mature stages move toward the open centre of the tubule before leaving it.

Interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, occupy spaces between tubules. They release testosterone into nearby blood vessels when they receive a suitable hormonal signal. This arrangement separates the site of hormone production from the site where sperm develop. A sperm cell is a reproductive cell; a Sertoli or interstitial cell supports reproduction through a different role. None of these terms names the entire testis.

The scrotum is the external pouch containing the testes. Its position and temperature-regulating responses help maintain conditions suited to sperm production. Temperature is one influence among several. If a model shows few developing sperm, examine the tubule environment, supporting cells and signals before identifying a cause. Evidence that testosterone is present does not establish that every stage of sperm development is working.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: The transport pathway
paragraphs: After leaving the seminiferous tubules, sperm pass into the epididymis, a long coiled duct beside the testis. Here they mature and can be stored. During ejaculation, muscular contractions move sperm into the vas deferens. Each vas joins a duct from a seminal vesicle to form an ejaculatory duct, which empties into the urethra. The urethra carries semen through the penis to the exterior.

The pathway connects different functions. Testicular tubules support production, the epididymis supports maturation and storage, and the remaining ducts support transport and delivery. Accessory secretions join along the route. Urine and semen use part of the same urethral passage at different times. The transport diagram therefore needs arrows showing direction, rather than lines that simply connect nearby structures.

Consider a fictional obstruction in a vas deferens. Sperm may still develop upstream while delivery through that duct is reduced. Testosterone can still enter the blood because hormone release follows a separate route. To test the transport explanation, compare evidence from before and after the proposed obstruction. A downstream sample alone cannot distinguish failed production from a blocked passage.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Semen and accessory glands
paragraphs: Semen is a mixture of sperm and secretions from reproductive glands. The paired seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder, which stores urine. They contribute much of its fluid and substances including fructose, which can support sperm energy needs. The prostate surrounds the upper part of the urethra below the bladder and adds fluid containing enzymes and other substances. These secretions change the transport medium; the glands themselves do not produce sperm.

Cowper glands, also called bulbourethral glands, lie near the base of the penis below the prostate. Their mucus helps lubricate the urethral passage and modify its local conditions. The exact composition of an ejaculate reflects contributions from several sites. It is therefore more useful to connect each gland with a contribution than to describe semen as the product of a single organ.

Suppose a model sample contains glandular fluid but no sperm. This observation shows that some secretory and delivery functions occurred. It leaves at least two broad possibilities: sperm production was reduced, or sperm did not reach the sampled passage. Follow the pathway and seek a further observation that distinguishes those explanations. Do not treat the presence of fluid as proof that every reproductive step is intact.

parts.title: Reproductive development and health
paragraphs: Early embryos have tissues that can develop along different paths. A gene is a region of DNA whose activity helps produce a biological product or effect. In a typical XY pathway, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome helps start testis development. It works through other genes and cells. SRY does not build every reproductive structure on its own.

Developing testes release testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone, called AMH. Testosterone supports the growth of certain internal ducts. Some target tissues convert it to DHT, a stronger androgen that helps shape typical external structures. AMH causes another set of embryonic ducts to shrink. Without these testis signals, those ducts can form the uterine tubes and uterus. Ovaries also develop through active gene networks. Their growth is not a process with no gene control.

A signal needs a target that can respond at the right time. A receptor is a cell component that detects a signal and helps start a response. Changes in genes, hormone supply, receptors or timing can alter development. A chromosome image shows only part of this pathway. It cannot establish every body feature, fertility outcome, health need or identity. In a fictional case, separate what was observed from what you inferred.

A sexually transmitted infection, or STI, can affect reproductive function after development. Infection may cause swelling and damage to a passage or its lining. Some infections cause few clear symptoms. Damage can make transport less effective, but infection does not always cause infertility. When judging an information programme, check its evidence and clear wording. Also consider privacy, access, community views, environmental effects, resources and cost. These include social, cultural, ethical and economic concerns.

parts.title: Gametes and chromosome sets
paragraphs: A chromosome carries a long DNA molecule with associated proteins. A set contains one representative of each chromosome type. Typical human body cells are diploid: they contain two sets, with 46 chromosomes in total. Gametes are haploid, carrying one set of 23. Fertilization combines two haploid contributions, restoring two sets in the zygote. This avoids doubling the number of sets in each generation.

A spermatogonium is an early germ cell that can divide by mitosis, the process that usually preserves chromosome sets in daughter cells. A cell entering sperm-producing meiosis becomes a primary spermatocyte. Before the meiotic divisions, it replicates its DNA. Each chromosome then consists of two joined sister chromatids. The cell still has 46 chromosomes and two sets, although its DNA amount has doubled.

Track sets and copies separately. Meiosis I separates corresponding homologous chromosomes, reducing each product to one set. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. A diagram should state whether its counts refer to the original cell, one daughter cell or all products combined. Calling a replicated primary spermatocyte tetraploid would confuse extra DNA copies with extra homologous sets.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Division and differentiation
paragraphs: One primary spermatocyte normally completes two meiotic divisions. Meiosis I produces two secondary spermatocytes, each with 23 duplicated chromosomes in the human model. Meiosis II separates the sister chromatids, producing four haploid spermatids. Each spermatid has 23 unduplicated chromosomes. The sequence reduces chromosome sets once, then separates the remaining copies without another round of DNA replication.

Spermatids must also change their structure. During differentiation, their nuclei become more compact, a flagellum develops, and excess cytoplasm is removed. The flagellum is the tail-like structure involved in movement. Mitochondria near its base support energy transfer. The acrosome is a specialized structure over part of the head that supports interaction with the oocyte's coverings. These changes produce spermatozoa, or differentiated sperm cells.

Differentiation changes cell form and function; it does not halve chromosome number again. Later maturation in the epididymis and changes within the reproductive tract support further functional readiness. A sperm may have the usual chromosome number yet show reduced movement or an impaired acrosome. Describe the affected step before predicting a downstream consequence. Shape, chromosome count and successful fertilization require different kinds of evidence.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Hormone sources and targets
paragraphs: Hormones coordinate sperm production with activity elsewhere in the body. The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. This signal stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release FSH and LH. FSH means follicle-stimulating hormone, and LH means luteinizing hormone. Their names reflect ovarian functions, but both also act in the testicular pathway.

FSH supports Sertoli-cell functions within the seminiferous tubules. LH stimulates interstitial cells to produce testosterone. Testosterone acts with other signals to support reproductive tissues and sperm development. It also influences several secondary sex characteristics during puberty, including changes in muscle, hair growth and voice. Primary sex characteristics are structures directly involved in reproduction. Secondary characteristics develop particularly during puberty and are not themselves gamete-producing or transport organs.

Keep source, signal, target and response in order. For example, write anterior pituitary → LH → interstitial cell → testosterone release. Testosterone then reaches responsive tissues through the blood. Its concentration alone does not reveal every target response. A cell without an effective receptor may respond weakly even when the signal is present. This distinction helps explain why one hormone measurement cannot diagnose an entire pathway.

GnRH reaches the anterior pituitary through connecting blood vessels. FSH and LH then travel in blood to their target tissues. They stimulate responses; they do not turn into testosterone or other reproductive hormones. A complete pathway therefore names the source, the signal carried in blood and the responding cell. It keeps hormone movement separate from sperm movement through a duct.

parts.title: Feedback and evidence
paragraphs: Negative feedback occurs when a response reduces the change that initiated it. In the testicular pathway, testosterone can reduce upstream hypothalamic and pituitary signalling. Sertoli cells also release inhibin, a signal that reduces pituitary FSH release. These feedback routes connect downstream activity with earlier control points. The word negative describes the direction of regulation, rather than judging the response as harmful.

Consider a synthetic comparison in which testosterone decreases while LH increases. Reduced testosterone feedback could permit more LH release. The pattern is consistent with reduced testicular production or response, rather than a simple absence of pituitary stimulation. It does not uniquely establish a cause: timing, receptor function and other evidence could alter the explanation. Compare repeated measurements collected under stated conditions.

A controlled variable is a condition kept similar while another factor is compared. In a model study, hold the measurement method and sampling interval constant. Predict what would happen to the upstream signal if feedback became weaker, then compare that prediction with the data. A useful explanation names the observed change, the feedback mechanism and one observation that would challenge it.

An anabolic steroid is a steroid substance with actions related to testosterone. An outside androgen signal can suppress upstream signals through negative feedback and reduce normal sperm production. This shows why more circulating androgen action need not mean more sperm. Human growth hormone, or hGH, is a protein hormone made by the pituitary. It is not a steroid, despite being grouped with steroids on one supplied slide.

Testosterone patterns can also change with age, health and other conditions. The term andropause is sometimes used for age-related changes, but it should not imply one abrupt, universal end to sperm production. A symptom such as tiredness has many possible explanations. In a scientific case, compare repeated measurements and the stated context rather than inferring a specific hormone condition from age or one symptom alone.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Ovaries and supporting tissues
paragraphs: An ovary contains developing oocytes and the tissues that support them. An oocyte is a developing female germ cell. A follicle contains that cell together with surrounding support cells. As a follicle develops, its cells and the oocyte change in coordinated ways. The follicle can contribute hormones to the blood, while the oocyte carries the chromosome contribution for possible fertilization.

Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte from a mature follicle. The remaining follicular tissue stays in the ovary and develops into the corpus luteum. This temporary endocrine structure releases progesterone and estrogen after ovulation. If it does not receive pregnancy-related support, it usually regresses. The released oocyte and the corpus luteum therefore have different locations, structures and roles.

Use the tissue boundary when labelling an image. A label pointing to the oocyte should identify the cell, while a follicle label includes its supporting tissue. A corpus-luteum label refers to tissue remaining after release. Confusing these labels makes later hormone explanations difficult. For example, progesterone production after ovulation does not require the released oocyte to remain inside the corpus luteum.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Transport and implantation surfaces
paragraphs: The Fallopian tubes, also called uterine tubes, extend from near the ovaries toward the uterus. Finger-like fimbriae near each ovarian end help direct the released oocyte toward the tube. Cilia are tiny moving projections on cells lining the passage. Together with muscular activity, they support transport. The ovary is close to the tube's opening but is not joined to it by a sealed internal duct.

Fertilization usually occurs within a uterine tube. An early developing conceptus then moves toward the uterus, a muscular organ with an inner lining called the endometrium. The endometrium changes across the reproductive cycle and can support implantation when receptive. The cervix forms the lower uterine opening into the vagina. The vagina receives semen during intercourse and forms part of the birth passage.

Trace the order of movement on a labelled diagram. Oocyte release, sperm transport, fertilization and implantation are distinct events. Evidence that ovulation occurred does not prove that the tube was open or that implantation followed. To investigate an obstruction, identify which events occur upstream and which require passage through the affected region. Keep the usual location of fertilization separate from the later implantation surface.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Oogenesis and meiotic pauses
paragraphs: Oogenesis is the development of oocytes. In humans, primary oocytes begin meiosis before birth, then pause in the first division. From puberty onward, some follicles develop during each reproductive cycle. An oocyte usually finishes meiosis I shortly before ovulation. The chromosomes separate, but the cytoplasm does not split equally. One large secondary oocyte forms, along with a small polar body.

The secondary oocyte begins meiosis II, then usually pauses at metaphase II. This is its stage when released at ovulation. It has one set of chromosomes, but each chromosome still has two joined sister chromatids. Sperm entry normally triggers the rest of meiosis II. The cytoplasm again splits unequally. The maternal and paternal chromosome sets can then come together. Polar bodies receive chromosomes but little cytoplasm. They usually do not become functional gametes.

Compare this sequence with spermatogenesis. Both use meiosis to reduce the number of chromosome sets. Spermatogenesis usually forms four similar-sized spermatids, which then change shape and mature. Oogenesis keeps most resources in one large cell and includes long pauses. Equal sharing of chromosomes does not require equal cell sizes. Count at a named stage: the secondary oocyte released at ovulation has 23 duplicated chromosomes. It has not yet finished meiosis II.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Structure and reproductive function
paragraphs: Reproduction needs working tissues, hormone support and an open route for transport. Cilia need a healthy lining to move an oocyte. Muscle activity also helps move it along the passage. A blockage may make it harder for gametes to meet or for an early conceptus to reach the uterus. Fertility describes a chance under stated conditions. It does not promise an outcome for one person.

Some infections cause inflammation, followed by scarring. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can contribute to pelvic inflammatory disease. This condition affects upper reproductive tissues. Scars may change a uterine tube's lining or block its passage. Follow the proposed chain: infection, then tissue damage, then an effect on transport. Each link needs evidence. Not every infection causes damage, and one person's reproductive outcome may have several causes.

Use the fictional cases to investigate production and transport without sharing personal information. Start with this question: can sperm production continue if a duct is blocked? Predict what you would see in the testis and in the passage. Next, record each case's tissue, signal and passage observations. Compare Case T with a case that has an open passage.

Case T has a blocked passage, yet retains observations of germ cells and their support. This means low delivery need not mean low production. Name another observation that could help tell these explanations apart. Then revise your explanation using the evidence. This online task shows your reasoning. It does not certify physical laboratory skills or live teamwork.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Two coordinated cycles
paragraphs: The ovarian cycle describes changes in follicles, ovulation and the corpus luteum. The uterine cycle describes changes in the endometrium. During the follicular phase, ovarian follicles develop while estrogen supports rebuilding of the uterine lining. After ovulation, the luteal phase begins as the remaining follicular tissue forms the corpus luteum. These ovarian events coordinate with a more secretory uterine lining.

Menstruation is the shedding of much of the functional endometrial lining. It commonly follows a decline in ovarian steroid support when pregnancy has not sustained the corpus luteum. Menstrual bleeding is usually counted as the start of a new cycle. Follicle recruitment can already be occurring around this transition, so biological events overlap rather than fitting into completely isolated boxes.

An illustrative 28-day cycle helps align events on a shared time axis, but real cycle lengths and ovulation timing vary. A diagram should name both the ovarian event and the uterine response. Saying that the ovary menstruates would place an event in the wrong organ. Saying that ovulation always occurs on one numbered day would treat an example schedule as a universal rule.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Follicle growth and changing feedback
paragraphs: At the start of a cycle, FSH from the pituitary supports follicle growth. Growing follicles release estrogen, which helps rebuild the uterine lining. Estrogen also acts on the brain and pituitary. At many stages, ovarian hormones reduce the release of FSH and LH. These two pituitary hormones are called gonadotropins. Changes in hormone supply and target sensitivity help coordinate follicle growth with the rest of the cycle.

Near ovulation, estrogen stays high long enough to change the feedback response. Under the conditions present at this stage, it increases activity in the hypothalamus and pituitary. A large rise in LH follows. This LH surge helps trigger ovulation and the formation of luteal tissue. Read this sequence in order: a sustained estrogen rise, then an LH surge, then the ovarian response.

Positive feedback strengthens the change that started the response. Here, rising estrogen helps increase an upstream signal instead of reducing it. Estrogen does not always have the same feedback effect. Its level, how long it stays high and the state of its targets all matter. On a pathway diagram, label each arrow as stimulation or inhibition. State the stage of the cycle so the arrow has a clear meaning.

Ovarian hormones also help bring about changes at puberty. Estrogen supports reproductive tissue growth and secondary changes such as breast development. Progesterone works with other signals to support tissues such as the uterine lining. An ovary or uterus is a primary reproductive structure; breast development is a secondary pubertal change. GnRH, FSH and LH act before the ovarian response, as they do in the testis pathway. Timing and growth vary. One visible trait cannot reveal the whole hormone pathway.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Corpus luteum and the endometrium
paragraphs: After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone and estrogen. Progesterone helps the endometrium maintain secretions and conditions that can support an implanting blastocyst. Trace the link from source to target: corpus luteum, then progesterone, then uterine lining. Ovarian hormones also reduce activity in the hypothalamus and pituitary through negative feedback. One tissue change in the ovary can therefore affect both the uterus and later hormone release.

Without support from an early pregnancy, the corpus luteum usually shrinks. Progesterone and estrogen levels fall. Much of the functional uterine lining then breaks down and is shed as menstrual bleeding. The lower hormone levels also reduce negative feedback on the brain and pituitary. FSH and LH release can change, helping support follicle activity in the next cycle.

Separate two questions. What helps maintain the lining after ovulation? Progesterone does. What helps maintain the corpus luteum in early pregnancy? A signal called hCG does; a later lesson explains its source and role. Keep the tissue, its hormone and its target separate. On a typical cycle graph, link falling ovarian hormones to loss of support for the lining. The graph shows an example pattern, not an exact schedule for everyone.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Graphs and cycle variation
paragraphs: A graph communicates a comparison only when its axes and units are clear. Put cycle day on the horizontal axis. Label the vertical axis for each hormone, including whether values are concentrations or relative indices. Separate scales are suitable when signals have different units or ranges. Equal-looking heights on two relative scales do not establish equal numbers of hormone molecules.

Use the supplied six-day dataset to build four labelled series. The highest sampled estrogen value is on day 12, followed by the highest sampled LH value on day 14. Progesterone is higher on day 21 and lower on day 28. This order fits follicular development, an ovulatory signalling interval and later luteal support followed by withdrawal. The data do not identify an exact event between sparsely sampled days.

Plan the investigation before reading it. State a question about event order and predict the relationship you expect. Plot or organize every supplied value using consistent scales. Support an explanation with two named values, then compare it with the alternative claim that a peak alone gives an exact ovulation time. More frequent sampling could improve temporal resolution. It would still not make this synthetic cycle a method for predicting an individual's fertile days.

Menopause marks the end of recurring menstrual cycles through the natural loss of ovarian follicular function. The transition can involve changing cycle patterns and altered ovarian hormone support. Reduced feedback can be associated with higher pituitary FSH, so not every hormone simply falls together. This change differs from temporary variation in one cycle. A classroom graph should describe the pattern without using one symptom or a single measurement to diagnose its cause.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Hormonal technologies and perspectives
paragraphs: Some methods reduce the chance of conception by changing hormone signals. A contraceptive formulation may reduce the pituitary signals that support ovulation. It may also affect cervical mucus or the uterine lining. The effects depend on the formulation. Start with the step being changed. Then ask what result was measured and how the study counted it.

Science and society shape each other. Better ways to measure hormones helped researchers test feedback models. People also wanted new ways to control conception. That need helped shape research and the methods it produced. A method can meet one need while raising other questions. Its biological effect does not settle questions about access, cost or privacy.

Consider a fictional information service. One format costs less; another offers private access and more explanation. Compare social effects, cultural views, environmental resource use, ethical duties and economic costs. A learner may first choose the cheaper format. Concern about privacy could change that choice. Explain the revised trade-off. Keep a value judgment separate from a claim about how a hormone works.

Conception control and STI prevention answer different questions. A method that suppresses ovulation does not block transfer of pathogens. A barrier method can reduce transfer by limiting contact, while uncovered skin can still permit transmission. Its effect depends on the method and use. A percentage describing pregnancy prevention does not also measure STI prevention. An evidence comparison must name which outcome was counted.

parts.title: Gametes meet
paragraphs: Fertilization joins the contributions of sperm and oocyte and activates a new developmental sequence. It usually occurs in a uterine tube after sperm have travelled through the vagina, cervix and uterus. Only a small fraction of sperm reach the region containing the oocyte. Transport, survival and functional readiness all affect that possibility, so arrival is already the result of several coordinated steps.

Capacitation refers to changes sperm undergo in the reproductive tract that prepare them for later interactions. A sperm must then interact with cells and coverings around the oocyte. The zona pellucida is a specialized extracellular coat surrounding the oocyte. The acrosome reaction involves changes and release of acrosomal contents that help sperm interact with these coverings. A moving sperm with an impaired acrosome may still have difficulty completing ordinary fertilization.

After successful interaction and membrane fusion, sperm entry helps trigger changes within the oocyte. These include completion of its paused meiotic division and responses that limit additional sperm entry. Keep these events separate in a sequence diagram. Sperm movement, interaction with coverings, membrane fusion and activation are different steps. Evidence that a sperm reached the oocyte does not prove that the later steps occurred.
parts.status: authored-core-prose-initial-science-review; figure/worked/check/advanced and exact-source second review pending

parts.title: Combining chromosome sets
paragraphs: The ovulated secondary oocyte usually pauses in meiosis II. Sperm entry helps trigger the rest of that division. The cell divides its cytoplasm unequally and forms another polar body. The maternal and paternal chromosome sets then occupy separate pronuclei. A pronucleus holds one gamete's chromosome set before the first embryonic division. Both sets are now within one cell.

In the usual human model, each gamete supplies 23 chromosomes. The two sets establish 46 chromosomes in a diploid zygote. A zygote is the single-cell stage formed by fertilization. Both DNA sets must be copied before the first mitotic division. That later division will divide the copies between cells. It does not add another gamete's chromosome set.

A polyspermy block helps prevent entry of more than one sperm. Small secretory structures near the oocyte surface are called cortical granules. On activation, they release contents that change the surrounding coat. This reduces further sperm interaction. Different species use different details of this process. In the human model, explain how limiting extra sperm helps protect the usual chromosome count.

parts.title: Cleavage and blastocyst formation
paragraphs: Cleavage consists of early mitotic divisions after fertilization. The resulting cells are called blastomeres. At first, the divisions split the existing cytoplasm into smaller cells. Cell number rises while overall size changes much less. The surrounding coat is still present. Thus, more cells do not yet mean a much larger conceptus. Later growth will add more total tissue.

The morula is a compact cluster of cells. Fluid then collects and the cells organize into a blastocyst. Its inner cell mass contributes to the embryo proper. The outer trophoblast contributes to supporting tissues and the placental interface. These groups have different roles and interact as development proceeds. Neither group is already a completed organ or an entire placenta.

The blastocyst leaves its coat before full contact with the uterine surface. One early embryo can also give rise to two embryos, producing monozygotic twins. Two separately fertilized oocytes produce dizygotic twins. Monozygotic twins may have shared or separate supporting membranes. Their common origin does not guarantee the same later traits. Mutations, gene use and conditions can still differ.

parts.title: Implantation and reproductive technology
paragraphs: Implantation occurs when a blastocyst attaches and embeds in receptive endometrium. It follows fertilization, early cell divisions and transport toward the uterus. Trophoblast takes part in contact with the uterine tissue and the developing exchange surface. Both the blastocyst and the uterine lining must be in a suitable state. Success at an earlier step does not guarantee this next event.

In vitro fertilization, or IVF, places fertilization outside the body. A simplified plan starts with obtaining oocytes. It then brings the gamete contributions together and supports early development. An embryo is transferred into the uterus. This places it at a later step in the usual pathway. Transfer itself does not prove that implantation or a continuing pregnancy will follow.

Check the denominator of a reported success rate. A rate per transfer counts only attempts that reached transfer. A rate per started cycle also counts earlier attempts that did not get that far. Check the endpoint too. A detected pregnancy and a live birth are different results. Use matching definitions and populations when comparing methods. Cost, access and values also matter.

Artificial insemination places sperm in the reproductive tract to help sperm reach an oocyte. Fertilization still occurs within the body if the required conditions are met. In vitro fertilization, or IVF, brings gametes together outside the body before a possible embryo transfer. Compare the location of fertilization and the barrier each method addresses. Neither method guarantees a pregnancy or a birth.

parts.title: A signal maintains the early pregnancy
paragraphs: Trophoblast releases human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, during early pregnancy. This signal helps maintain the corpus luteum. The ovarian tissue can then keep producing progesterone and estrogen instead of regressing. Those hormones help support the uterine environment. The pathway connects three distinct roles: the source of a signal, the tissue receiving it and the tissue response that follows.

hCG can act at a receptor also used by LH. This does not make them the same hormone. Their main sources differ. A rise in hCG does not mean the anterior pituitary released more LH. In the diagram, trace trophoblast → hCG → corpus luteum → continued steroid release. Then follow progesterone to responsive uterine tissue. Name each source and target.

Later, the placenta produces much of the steroid support. To make some hormones, it uses starting materials supplied by maternal and fetal tissues. The source of a hormone can therefore change with time. A high late-pregnancy value does not prove that an ovary supplied it. Match the measured signal to the stage and source before drawing a conclusion about development.

parts.title: Gastrulation establishes layers
paragraphs: Gastrulation reorganizes the early embryo to establish three primary germ layers. A germ layer is a developing cell population that contributes to later tissues. Cells change position through coordinated movements, including migration through a region called the primitive streak. The resulting ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm occupy different relationships within the developing body plan. Position and communication help influence what these cells later become.

Cell differentiation is the process through which cells become specialized. It involves changes in the genes used and the products made, rather than requiring every cell to inherit a completely different genome. Signals from neighbouring cells and the surrounding environment influence development. Cells also change their shape, attachment and movement. Together, these processes help organize tissue patterns and begin the formation of body structures.

Morphogenesis means the development of biological form. It includes movements, folding and coordinated growth that shape structures, rather than simply increasing cell number. Gastrulation is therefore different from early cleavage: cleavage at first partitions cells, while gastrulation reorganizes tissue relationships. Draw arrows that represent cell movement when explaining a germ-layer diagram. A static list of three layer names cannot show how the layers become established.

parts.title: Layer-to-tissue relationships
paragraphs: Ectoderm contributes to the epidermis, the skin's outer lining, and to the nervous system. Part of this layer forms the neural tube, which contributes to the brain and spinal cord. Other regions follow different paths. Cells from one early layer can thus become tissues with very different adult roles. Their final form depends on later signals and interactions too.

Mesoderm contributes to muscle, much of the skeleton, blood and many reproductive structures. Endoderm contributes to the inner linings of the digestive and respiratory systems. It also contributes to some glands. Examples include pancreatic endocrine tissue and thyroid follicular cells. These examples identify tissue origins. They do not mean that every part of a whole organ has one origin.

Endocrine tissues come from more than one layer. Pituitary tissues have ectodermal origins; the adrenal cortex comes from mesoderm. A digestive organ also has more than an inner lining. Its muscle and support tissues have mesodermal contributions. When mapping an organ, name the tissue being traced. This makes the layer map useful without treating a complex organ as a single cell type.

parts.title: Developmental evidence
paragraphs: Evidence can come from cells, tissue markers, organ shape or body function. An observation is a recorded result. A model is a simpler account used to explain or predict such results. One finding may fit several accounts. A changed tissue marker might reflect changed cell type, fewer cells or a problem with the way the marker was measured.

Time helps test a proposed cause. An exposure after a tissue formed cannot explain a result by claiming it stopped that earlier event. It could still affect later growth or function. First state which process is active at the time. Then ask what was measured. A marker change needs more evidence before it can be linked to a change in an organ.

A causal limit is a boundary on what evidence can show about cause. A non-human model can support a mechanism without giving a human risk value. Groups in an observational study may differ in other relevant ways. A graph with an unnamed vertical axis cannot establish a specific hormone curve. Check the source, measure, time, comparison and alternatives before explaining an effect.

parts.title: Support membranes
paragraphs: Extraembryonic structures lie outside the embryo proper and support its development. The amnion forms the membrane around the fluid-filled amniotic space. Amniotic fluid cushions movement and contributes to a protected environment in which the fetus can move and develop. The chorion forms an outer membrane and contributes to the fetal side of the placental interface. These membranes have distinct positions and functions.

The placenta combines interacting fetal and maternal components. Chorionic structures grow near maternal tissues and blood spaces, creating an exchange surface. The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta and contains fetal blood vessels embedded in supporting tissue. It is not a tube carrying maternal blood directly into the fetus. Trace which structure belongs to the fetal circulation when reading the connection.

The human allantois is a small early extension associated with the connecting region and development near the future bladder. Its relationships differ from the large waste-storage structure found in some egg-laying vertebrates. The yolk sac also has early developmental roles, including contributions to early blood formation and the germ-cell pathway; a human embryo does not depend on a large stored yolk supply. Compare human support structures by function without assuming that every species uses them identically.

parts.title: Maternal and fetal circulation
paragraphs: At the placenta, maternal and fetal blood usually remain in separate circuits. Maternal blood enters spaces near the chorionic villi. Fetal blood flows through vessels inside these exchange structures. Thin layers of tissue keep the two blood supplies apart while allowing materials to cross. A large surface area helps exchange. Diffusion moves materials down a concentration or partial-pressure gradient. Other forms of transport also help materials cross the placenta.

Follow the materials and vessels separately. Oxygen and nutrients can move toward fetal blood. Carbon dioxide and some wastes can move toward maternal blood. The umbilical arteries carry blood from the fetus to the placenta. The umbilical vein carries blood back to the fetus. An artery carries blood away from the fetal heart; a vein carries it toward the heart. These names describe direction, not a fixed oxygen level.

The placenta controls exchange, but it does not block every substance. Transfer depends on the substance, the gradient, transport processes and the tissues. First ask whether a substance crosses. Then ask what effect it has. Crossing alone does not prove harm. To judge an effect, examine the amount, timing, how the substance is processed and the target's response. Draw two separate blood circuits with exchange between them, not one continuous maternal-to-fetal vessel.

parts.title: Organ formation across development
paragraphs: Organogenesis is the formation of organ structures from developing tissues. Growth adds size or cells. Differentiation changes cell roles, while morphogenesis changes form. These processes overlap. An early embryo is not simply a finished miniature body that gets larger. Cells must move, fold, respond to signals and form new tissue patterns. These changes help build each working system.

Always state where a developmental clock starts. Time since fertilization begins at gamete union. Obstetric gestational age is counted from the last menstrual period's start. In a typical example, it is about two weeks greater. The embryonic period includes major early body patterning. The fetal period begins after roughly eight weeks from fertilization, with growth and maturation continuing.

During the first trimester, major events include nervous-system, heart, blood-vessel and limb development. During the second, growth, movement and changes in bone and nervous tissue continue. The third includes more growth, energy storage and lung and brain maturation. These are overlapping patterns, not one exact schedule. As the fetus grows, nearby organs can shift, helping explain some bladder, breathing or digestive effects.

Neurulation helps establish the early central nervous system. A region of ectoderm thickens into the neural plate. It folds to form a groove, and the folds join to form the neural tube. This tube gives rise to the brain and spinal cord. The process begins during early embryonic development, around the third week after fertilization, and continues through later stages. A folded tube is an early structure, not a finished working nervous system.

parts.title: Environmental influence and evidence
paragraphs: A teratogen is an agent that can disrupt prenatal development under certain conditions. The effect depends on the agent, dose, route, timing and response. Dose is the amount reaching the relevant system. Route is how it enters. The same outside exposure can lead to different amounts inside the body. This helps explain why an agent's name alone cannot predict an outcome.

Alcohol, some infections, some medicines and other agents can affect development. Explain the evidence and the process without assigning blame or claiming one certain result. Tissue formation can create an early sensitive period. Later growth or brain maturation can create other periods of concern. A study of one stage therefore does not settle every question about the same exposure at another stage.

A confounder is another difference between groups that could help explain their results. An exposed group may differ in more than the exposure itself. A controlled model can help isolate a mechanism, but may not apply directly to humans. Compare the groups, time and measured outcome. State what the result supports and one finding that would strengthen or challenge the claim.

parts.title: Labour and positive feedback
paragraphs: Parturition means labour and birth. Hormonal, local and mechanical signals act together during this process. Progesterone helps maintain pregnancy, while changes in tissue response to it help prepare for labour. In humans, progesterone action can decline without a large fall in its blood level. A model that requires that fall in every human birth leaves out this important distinction.

Prostaglandins are local signals that help change the cervix and support contractions. Neurons in the hypothalamus make oxytocin. The posterior pituitary releases it into the blood, where it can reach responsive uterine tissue. Contractions press the fetus toward the cervix. Stretch there sends sensory signals that can support more oxytocin release and stronger contractions. Each arrow represents a stated action.

This loop is positive feedback because the response reinforces the starting stretch. Delivery removes that stimulus and provides an endpoint. The loop explains one part of labour, not every cause of its onset or progress. If stretch and contraction rise together on a graph, the pattern fits the model. Explaining cause still requires the pathway and evidence about other active processes.

Prostaglandins are lipid signals that can act locally in reproductive tissues. Some support cervical change and uterine contraction during labour. Their effects depend on the signal, receptor and tissue. Birth therefore involves more than a single oxytocin arrow. Changing tissue responses and other signals help establish the conditions in which the reinforcing loop operates. The source diagram is a useful model when these limits are stated.

parts.title: Birth and the transition
paragraphs: Labour takes place in stages. First, the cervix, the lower opening of the uterus, widens. This is cervical dilation. Contractions and tissue changes help it progress. Next, delivery moves the fetus through the birth passage. The placenta then separates and is expelled. These broad stages help explain birth. They are not an exact schedule for one person or instructions for clinical care.

Before birth, gases and wastes are exchanged through the placenta. After birth, the newborn must move air through the lungs as placental exchange ends. Blood flow must also adapt. Follow the change in the main site of gas exchange: from the placenta before birth to the lungs afterward. Growth and maturation before birth help prepare the lungs and other tissues for this transition.

Delivery of the placenta also removes a source of steroid hormones. Their levels fall, changing feedback and tissue responses after pregnancy. Other hormone-producing tissues still matter. In a fictional case where the ovaries are also removed, major ovarian hormone sources are lost as well. Start by naming each lost source. Then explain that its hormone supply will decline. These observations alone cannot specify a treatment or when it should begin.

parts.title: Milk synthesis and release
paragraphs: Lactation includes making milk and moving it toward the nipple. The anterior pituitary releases prolactin, which supports milk synthesis in mammary cells. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin. It makes myoepithelial cells contract around milk-producing structures. These are contractile support cells. Their action helps push milk into the ducts. Making milk and releasing it thus depend on different target responses.

Suckling provides sensory input that supports both pathways. Prolactin helps maintain production, while oxytocin supports milk ejection. During pregnancy, hormones help the mammary tissue develop. After the placenta is delivered, steroid levels fall. This supports much greater milk synthesis after birth. The same tissue can respond differently before and after birth because its hormonal context changes.

Trace one pathway at a time. For ejection, connect suckling, sensory input, hypothalamic activity, oxytocin release and target-cell contraction. For synthesis, identify prolactin and the cells making milk. A model can show milk present in the gland but weak movement into the ducts. This points to a different step from low synthesis. The observation alone does not diagnose a person's situation.

parts.title: Technologies, infertility and perspectives
paragraphs: Different technologies act at different reproductive steps. A barrier reduces chances for gametes to meet. A hormonal method changes signals or tissue conditions. Surgery can interrupt a vas deferens or uterine tube and change transport. For each method, name the affected step and measured result. Its mechanism alone does not establish effectiveness under all use conditions or for all people.

An approach to infertility must match the cause. Hormone support may help a signalling problem if the target tissue can respond. Restoring a passage may help when other needed structures and cells still function. IVF places fertilization outside the body and can bypass some transport barriers. These approaches can expand capability, but none guarantees every later step of conception and development.

Biological and social roles can also differ. Sperm and oocyte contributors supply genes; a gestational carrier supports prenatal development. Intended or social parents take other roles, which may overlap. These facts do not rank families or establish a universal legal definition. For a fictional service, compare evidence, access, cultural views, environmental demands, ethics and costs. Revise its plan after considering a contrasting perspective.

A success percentage needs a stated outcome and denominator. Suppose a fictional service records 12 live births after 30 transfers from 50 started cycles. The live-birth percentage is 12/30×100=40% per transfer, but 12/50×100=24% per started cycle. Cycles that did not reach transfer remain in the second denominator. Compare reports using the same outcome, time interval and starting population.

parts.title: Investigating and communicating a claim
paragraphs: A well-designed investigation starts with a testable question and an explicit comparison. In the supplied non-human cell model, compare an unexposed group with a group exposed to agent X at each of two developmental stages. Keep the agent amount, exposure duration, measurement method and culture conditions comparable. The measured outcome is marker M, a fictional biological indicator. It is not a diagnosed human developmental condition.

Record the four counts before reading them. At the early stage, 4 of 40 unexposed samples and 20 of 40 exposed samples show the marker. Their proportions are 0.10 and 0.50, a difference of 0.40. At the later stage, the proportions are 5/40=0.125 and 9/40=0.225, a difference of 0.10. The larger early contrast supports a stage-related difference in this model's response.

Now examine the alternative claim that the experiment gives a precise human risk. The model uses a different biological system and an indirect endpoint, so that conclusion goes beyond its evidence. Replication, group allocation, uncertainty and a link between the marker and organ development would strengthen the investigation. Communicate your comparison with labelled values, explain a plausible mechanism, evaluate the alternative and revise your claim. Independent digital reasoning does not certify physical laboratory performance or live collaboration.
